title: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and corticostriatal deficits revealed by neuroimaging

claims.statement: Whether methamphetamine use, as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans has not been established: lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found, but the measures available cannot distinguish loss of nerve terminals from reversible down-regulation, some markers return toward normal with abstinence, and the pattern differs from that of Parkinson's disease.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable: no study has counted dopamine neurons or terminals quantitatively in human users.

claims.statement: Structural MRI studies report less grey matter in some frontal, cingulate, insular and temporal regions in people with methamphetamine dependence than in controls, but in the study that separated tobacco smoking, non-using smokers also had less orbitofrontal grey matter than non-smokers, and only 4 of 10 regional differences remained when users were compared with smoking controls. An earlier report of 7.8% smaller hippocampi was not reproduced by the same laboratory, and memory scores were never compared between groups in that report.
claims.magnitude: Thompson et al. (2004; 22 vs 21): cingulate–paralimbic grey matter −11.3%, hippocampus −7.8%, white matter +7.0%. Morales et al. (2012): 10 clusters smaller vs non-smoking controls; 4 vs smoking controls; orbitofrontal smaller in smoking controls too; no dose–response.

claims.statement: Non-using biological siblings of people with stimulant dependence share some fronto-striatal brain-structure differences and poorer inhibitory control with their dependent siblings, which indicates that some differences observed in people who use stimulants predate drug use; most dependent participants in that study used cocaine rather than methamphetamine.
